CHAPTER V. THE OLD CHURCH

I followed him deep into the pine-forest. Neither of us said much while
yet the sacred gloom of it closed us round. We came to larger and yet
larger trees--older, and more individual, some of them grotesque with
age. Then the forest grew thinner.

“You see that hawthorn?” said my guide at length, pointing with his
beak.

I looked where the wood melted away on the edge of an open heath.

“I see a gnarled old man, with a great white head,” I answered.

“Look again,” he rejoined: “it is a hawthorn.”

“It seems indeed an ancient hawthorn; but this is not the season for the
hawthorn to blossom!” I objected.

“The season for the hawthorn to blossom,” he replied, “is when the
hawthorn blossoms. That tree is in the ruins of the church on your
home-farm. You were going to give some directions to the bailiff about
its churchyard, were you not, the morning of the thunder?”

“I was going to tell him I wanted it turned into a wilderness of
rose-trees, and that the plough must never come within three yards of
it.”

“Listen!” said the raven, seeming to hold his breath.

I listened, and heard--was it the sighing of a far-off musical wind--or
the ghost of a music that had once been glad? Or did I indeed hear
anything?

“They go there still,” said the raven.

“Who goes there? and where do they go?” I asked.

“Some of the people who used to pray there, go to the ruins still,” he
replied. “But they will not go much longer, I think.”

“What makes them go now?”

“They need help from each other to get their thinking done, and their
feelings hatched, so they talk and sing together; and then, they say,
the big thought floats out of their hearts like a great ship out of the
river at high water.”

“Do they pray as well as sing?”

“No; they have found that each can best pray in his own silent
heart.--Some people are always at their prayers.--Look! look! There goes
one!”

He pointed right up into the air. A snow-white pigeon was mounting, with
quick and yet quicker wing-flap, the unseen spiral of an ethereal stair.
The sunshine flashed quivering from its wings.

“I see a pigeon!” I said.

“Of course you see a pigeon,” rejoined the raven, “for there is the
pigeon! I see a prayer on its way.--I wonder now what heart is that
dove’s mother! Some one may have come awake in my cemetery!”

“How can a pigeon be a prayer?” I said. “I understand, of course, how
it should be a fit symbol or likeness for one; but a live pigeon to come
out of a heart!”

“It MUST puzzle you! It cannot fail to do so!”

“A prayer is a thought, a thing spiritual!” I pursued.

“Very true! But if you understood any world besides your own, you would
understand your own much better.--When a heart is really alive, then it
is able to think live things. There is one heart all whose thoughts
are strong, happy creatures, and whose very dreams are lives. When some
pray, they lift heavy thoughts from the ground, only to drop them on it
again; others send up their prayers in living shapes, this or that, the
nearest likeness to each. All live things were thoughts to begin with,
and are fit therefore to be used by those that think. When one says to
the great Thinker:--‘Here is one of thy thoughts: I am thinking it now!’
that is a prayer--a word to the big heart from one of its own little
hearts.--Look, there is another!”

This time the raven pointed his beak downward--to something at the foot
of a block of granite. I looked, and saw a little flower. I had never
seen one like it before, and cannot utter the feeling it woke in me by
its gracious, trusting form, its colour, and its odour as of a new world
that was yet the old. I can only say that it suggested an anemone, was
of a pale rose-hue, and had a golden heart.

“That is a prayer-flower,” said the raven.

“I never saw such a flower before!” I rejoined.

“There is no other such. Not one prayer-flower is ever quite like
another,” he returned.

“How do you know it a prayer-flower?” I asked.

“By the expression of it,” he answered. “More than that I cannot tell
you. If you know it, you know it; if you do not, you do not.”

“Could you not teach me to know a prayer-flower when I see it?” I said.

“I could not. But if I could, what better would you be? you would not
know it of YOURSELF and ITself! Why know the name of a thing when the
thing itself you do not know? Whose work is it but your own to open your
eyes? But indeed the business of the universe is to make such a fool of
you that you will know yourself for one, and so begin to be wise!”

But I did see that the flower was different from any flower I had ever
seen before; therefore I knew that I must be seeing a shadow of the
prayer in it; and a great awe came over me to think of the heart
listening to the flower.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’
[Reference Rewrite]: “No room. Full up.”

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

An instant before, the torrential Victorian night had been a blur of freezing misery; now, my senses sharpened into jagged relief. The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

"Follow," the raven commanded, his voice cutting through the encroaching silence.

We moved deeper into the pine forest, the canopy thickening until the sacred gloom wrapped around us like a heavy cloak. Neither of us spoke; the weight of the journey demanded a discipline beyond mere words. As we advanced, the trees grew larger, older, their forms becoming increasingly individualistic, some twisted into grotesque silhouettes by centuries of wind and decay. Eventually, the dense timber gave way to a clearing, the forest thinning into an open expanse of heath.

"You see that hawthorn?" the guide asked, extending a sharp beak toward the edge of the woods.

I scanned the landscape where the trees dissolved into scrubland. "I see a gnarled old man with a great white head," I replied, my gaze fixed on the solitary, skeletal shape.

"Look again," the raven corrected. "It is a hawthorn."

"It appears to be an ancient specimen," I conceded, though skepticism lingered. "Yet this is not the season for blossoms!"

"The season for the hawthorn to blossom," the bird stated flatly, "is precisely when the hawthorn blossoms. That specific tree stands in the ruins of the church on your home farm. Recall the morning of the thunder; you intended to give the bailiff directions regarding its churchyard, did you not?"

"I was going to instruct him to transform it into a wilderness of rose-trees, ensuring the plough never came within three yards of the site."

"Listen!" the raven suddenly halted, holding his breath as if straining against a gale.

I strained my ears. Was it the sighing of a distant wind, carrying the ghost of music long forgotten? Or was I hearing nothing at all?

"They go there still," the raven whispered.

"Who goes there? And where do they go?" I asked, turning back to the creature.

"Some of the people who once prayed there continue to visit the ruins," he replied. "But I suspect they will not remain much longer."

"What compels them to go now?"

"They require assistance from one another to complete their thinking and hatch their feelings," the raven explained. "They gather to talk and sing. In doing so, they claim the great thought floats out of their hearts like a massive vessel leaving a river at high tide."

"Do they pray alongside their singing?"

"No. They have discovered that each person prays most effectively in their own silent heart. Observe—there goes one!"

He pointed upward. A snow-white pigeon mounted the sky, its wingbeats accelerating into a rapid, spiraling ascent—an ethereal staircase ascending into the sun. Light flashed quivering off its feathers.

"I see a pigeon," I said.

"Of course you see a pigeon," the raven retorted. "For there is the pigeon! But I see a prayer in transit. I wonder now what heart serves as that dove's mother. Perhaps someone has awakened in my cemetery."

"How can a pigeon constitute a prayer?" I pressed. "I understand how it might serve as a symbolic likeness, but a living bird emerging directly from a heart?"

"It MUST puzzle you! It cannot fail to do so!"

"A prayer is a thought, a purely spiritual entity!" I insisted.

"Very true! But if you comprehended any world besides your own, you would understand your own much better. When a heart is truly alive, it generates living thoughts. Consider one heart whose thoughts are strong, happy creatures, and whose dreams are actual lives. Some pray by lifting heavy burdens from the earth only to drop them back upon it; others launch their petitions in living shapes—the closest approximation available. All living things began as thoughts and are therefore suitable tools for those who think. When one addresses the Great Thinker: 'Here is one of thy thoughts: I am thinking it now!' that constitutes a prayer—a message from one of its own small hearts to the big heart. Look, there is another!"

This time, the raven directed his beak downward, toward a cluster of granite blocks at our feet. I looked and saw a tiny flower. It was unlike anything I had ever encountered, evoking a sensation of grace and trust, a color palette suggesting a new world that remained fundamentally familiar. It resembled an anemone, possessing a pale rose hue and a golden center.

"That is a prayer-flower," the raven declared.

"I have never seen such a flower before!" I rejoined.

"There is no other such. Not one prayer-flower is ever exactly alike," he returned.

"How do you distinguish a prayer-flower?" I asked.

"By its expression," he answered simply. "Beyond that, I cannot explain. If you recognize it, you recognize it; if you do not, you do not."

"Could you not teach me to identify a prayer-flower when I encounter it?"

"I could not. But if I could, what greater purpose would you serve? You would not know it through YOURSELF and ITSELF! Why learn the name of a thing when you do not truly know the thing itself? Whose responsibility is it but yours to open your eyes? Indeed, the business of the universe is to reduce you to such a state of folly that you realize you are one, and thus begin to be wise!"

Nevertheless, I acknowledged that the flower differed from any flora I had previously observed. Therefore, I knew I was witnessing a shadow of the prayer contained within it. A profound awe washed over me as I contemplated the vast heart listening to the flower.
